strengths: The core idea—contrastive learning between proprioceptive and privileged states (available via the common asymmetric actor-critic setup) to improve proprioceptive representations—is simple, well-motivated, and clearly explained with a SimSiam-style formulation and zero-masking to align dimensionality.

The paper contributes SRL4Humanoid, a modular open-source framework implementing multiple representative SRL paradigms (reconstruction-based VAE, dynamics-modeling SPR, contrastive SimSiam) alongside PvP, which could be a useful community resource for systematic study of SRL in humanoid RL.

Experimental evaluation is reasonably broad for a single-robot study: two distinct WBC tasks (velocity tracking and motion imitation), four baseline comparisons, and six targeted ablations/analyses (training-time proportion, training-data proportion, which encoder benefits from SRL, computational overhead, and Sim2Sim/real-robot validation).

Practical, non-obvious findings are reported, such as SRL applied to the value encoder causing training collapse in the velocity task, and the need for an interval-update mechanism to prevent premature convergence to local optima — these provide actionable guidance beyond just the headline result.
The approach is validated beyond simulation with Sim2Sim (MuJoCo) and real hardware deployment on the LimX Oli humanoid, which is more convincing than simulation-only evaluation.
weaknesses: Evaluation is confined to a single robot platform (LimX Oli) and only two tasks (velocity tracking, motion imitation); no manipulation or more diverse terrain/task settings are tested despite the paper's broader WBC framing, limiting evidence for generality.

The comparison against baselines (VAE, SPR, SimSiam) may not isolate the actual source of PvP's gains: baselines only use proprioceptive-only contrastive/reconstruction objectives, while PvP additionally exploits privileged information. A control baseline that simply concatenates or predicts privileged features into the encoder without contrastive structure (or that gives baselines access to the same privileged signal) is missing, making it hard to attribute improvement specifically to the contrastive mechanism rather than to added information access.

Real-world evaluation (Section 5.2.6, Figure 1c/11) is qualitative only (image sequences), without quantitative real-robot metrics (e.g., tracking error, energy consumption, failure rate), weakening claims of "reliable real-world deployment."

No comparison to strong non-SRL, task-specific humanoid WBC baselines (e.g., the cited BeyondMimic, HugWBC) is provided to contextualize whether PvP-enhanced PPO is competitive with state-of-the-art absolute performance, only relative gains over an internal PPO baseline are shown.

The number of random seeds used to generate the shown mean/std shaded regions is not explicitly stated, and no significance testing is reported, making it harder to assess robustness of the reported improvements.

Minor clarity issues: some figures (e.g., Fig. 2) have small/unclear labels ("Poicy Encoder"), and detailed justification for specific design choices (e.g., why root linear velocity/orientation specifically chosen as privileged targets, why interval of 50 is optimal) is largely empirical/ad hoc rather than principled.

strengths: The paper addresses a practical and relevant problem—sample-inefficient RL for humanoid whole-body control—and proposes a reasonably motivated solution (contrastive alignment between proprioceptive and privileged representations).

The SRL4Humanoid framework is a useful engineering contribution that decouples SRL and RL updates and implements several representative SRL baselines (VAE, SPR, SimSiam) in a unified codebase, which could aid reproducibility if released.

The ablation studies are relatively thorough within the chosen setting: impact of SRL update interval, proportion of training data used, and whether SRL loss is applied to policy vs. value encoder, along with a 'training collapse' observation for value-encoder SRL that is a useful practical finding.
Real robot qualitative deployment (LimX Oli) and Sim2Sim validation on MuJoCo are included, going beyond pure simulation results.

The negative cosine similarity / SimSiam-style contrastive formulation is simple, and the zero-masking trick to unify proprioceptive/privileged dimensions is a lightweight architectural idea that does not require hand-crafted augmentations.
weaknesses: Evaluation breadth is very limited: all experiments are run on a single robot platform (LimX Oli) and only two tasks (velocity tracking and one motion-imitation benchmark), which makes it hard to judge generality of the claimed gains across humanoid morphologies or more diverse/dynamic skills (e.g., terrain traversal, manipulation, disturbance rejection) that are common in the cited literature (HugWBC, BeyondMimic, etc.).

Real-world evaluation is only qualitative (video frames/snapshots); no quantitative real-robot metrics (tracking error, success rate, energy use, action smoothness) are reported, so the claim of improved 'reliability in real-world deployment' is not rigorously substantiated.

The core technical novelty is incremental: it largely amounts to applying a SimSiam-style contrastive loss between teacher (privileged) and student (proprioceptive) representations, an idea closely related to prior asymmetric actor-critic and PIM-style approaches (e.g., [18]); the delta over this prior work (using privileged state instead of a single modality) is a relatively small conceptual step.

Statistical rigor is unclear: the number of random seeds per curve, significance testing, and variance reporting beyond shaded bands are not clearly specified, making it difficult to assess whether the large margin over baselines (especially on velocity tracking) is robust or possibly due to favorable hyperparameter search specifically tuned for PvP versus baselines.

The baselines compared (VAE, SPR, SimSiam with hand-designed augmentations) are reasonable but somewhat dated/generic; no comparison is made to more recent, task-specific SRL or privileged-learning approaches for legged/humanoid control beyond citation, so it's unclear how PvP stacks up against stronger contemporary alternatives.

The interval-update mechanism (Eq. 6) and the finding that continuous SRL updates can hurt performance are presented somewhat ad hoc, with limited theoretical justification for why this instability occurs and why 50 steps specifically is optimal, beyond empirical tuning.

strengths: The core idea—applying SimSiam-style contrastive learning between proprioceptive and privileged states within the standard asymmetric actor-critic paradigm for humanoid WBC—is simple, well-motivated, and effectively exploits the natural sim-only privileged information without requiring hand-crafted data augmentations, unlike the VAE/SPR baselines that need augmentation search.

The paper contributes SRL4Humanoid, a unified, modular open-source framework implementing multiple representative SRL paradigms (reconstruction/VAE, dynamics modeling/SPR, contrastive/SimSiam, and PvP) under a common RL backbone, which is a useful artifact for reproducibility and future community research.

The empirical study is fairly systematic and goes beyond a single headline comparison: it examines the effect of SRL update interval, training data proportion, which network (policy vs. value encoder) benefits from the SRL loss, and computational overhead, yielding practically useful findings (e.g., the interval-update trick to avoid early-training collapse, and that applying SRL to the value encoder can destabilize training).

Real-robot deployment and Sim2Sim (MuJoCo) validation on the LimX Oli platform for both velocity tracking and motion imitation provide evidence the learned policies transfer beyond the training simulator, which is important for WBC research credibility.
Clear ablations on key sub-metrics (e.g., tracking accuracy, action smoothness) rather than only the aggregate reward, giving a more granular picture of where PvP helps.
weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to a single humanoid platform (LimX Oli) and only two tasks (velocity tracking on flat terrain, motion imitation), which constrains claims about general applicability to more diverse morphologies, terrains, or contact-rich manipulation/loco-manipulation tasks common in humanoid WBC research.

The paper omits comparison to closely related teacher-student/privileged-information distillation approaches (e.g., RMA-style or DAgger-based privileged learning) that are widely used baselines for exploiting privileged simulator states in legged/humanoid RL; only reconstruction-, dynamics-, and contrastive-based SRL baselines are considered, leaving an important class of competing methods unaddressed.

The benefit of PvP appears markedly stronger on the velocity-tracking task than on the motion-imitation task (Figure 5), where several baselines are competitive or occasionally comparable to PvP; the abstract's claim of 'significantly improves' across tasks is somewhat stronger than what the mimic-task curves show.

The interval-update mechanism (Eq. 6) and the 'training collapse' phenomenon (Fig. 10) are presented mainly as empirical observations without deeper analysis of the underlying cause (e.g., is it a critic value-scale mismatch, representation collapse, or reward misalignment?), leaving the fix feeling somewhat ad hoc despite being practically useful.

Statistical rigor is not fully clear: the number of random seeds used to produce the shown mean/std bands is not stated, and no significance tests are reported, making it harder to assess how robust the reported gains are.

The ablation on which encoder benefits more from SRL (Section 5.2.4) is only shown for SimSiam and VAE, not for the paper's main proposed method PvP itself, leaving a gap in validating this specific design choice for the core contribution.

Some experimental design choices (e.g., which privileged features are used for PvP per task, zero-masking scheme) are fixed rather than ablated, so it is unclear how sensitive PvP's gains are to the particular choice of privileged information used for contrastive learning.

strengths: Proposes a simple, well-motivated contrastive learning approach (PvP) that exploits complementary information between proprioceptive and privileged states, avoiding hand-crafted data augmentations that are typically needed by contrastive SRL methods.

Introduces SRL4Humanoid, a unified, modular open-source benchmarking framework for systematically comparing SRL methods (reconstruction-based VAE, dynamics-modeling SPR, contrastive SimSiam) in humanoid WBC RL, which could be a useful community resource for reproducible research.

Extensive empirical study addressing multiple practical research questions (update interval, training data proportion, which encoder to apply SRL to, computational overhead), going beyond a single headline result to provide actionable design guidance.

Evaluation spans two distinct benchmark tasks (velocity tracking and motion imitation) plus appendix experiments on additional terrain and a different robot platform (Unitree G1), as well as real-world hardware deployment and Sim2Sim validation on MuJoCo, which strengthens claims about the practical usefulness of the method.

Comparison against teacher-student distillation (TSD) baselines in the appendix, clarifying PvP's conceptual advantage of jointly evolving representation and policy rather than relying on a fixed pretrained teacher.

Ablation on the loss weighting coefficient and on applying SRL loss to policy vs. value encoder provides useful mechanistic insight (e.g., collapse observed when applying SRL to value encoder in velocity task).
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is relatively incremental: it is essentially SimSiam contrastive learning applied to a privileged/proprioceptive pair with zero-masking, closely resembling existing contrastive-privileged-information approaches (e.g., PIM) with an added second modality; the novelty relative to combining known asymmetric actor-critic and contrastive SSL ideas is limited and could be more clearly delineated from prior work such as PIM and teacher-student distillation.

Real-robot evaluation (Q6, Figure 1c) is only qualitatively illustrated with a handful of frames and referenced supplementary videos, without any quantitative real-world metrics (e.g., tracking error, success rate, robustness under disturbance), limiting the strength of claims about real-world deployment reliability.

All main experiments are conducted on a single primary robot (LimX Oli) with only two tasks; while appendix adds a second robot (Unitree G1) and a rough-terrain variant, the number of seeds/runs is not clearly reported and statistical significance of differences (e.g., error bars appear as shaded std across few seeds) is not rigorously established.

The interval-update mechanism (Eq. 6, indicator function to update SRL loss every T steps) is introduced somewhat ad hoc based on an informally described training collapse observation, without a systematic ablation showing how T was selected and how sensitive results are to it beyond Figure 8's coarse sweep.

Baseline hyperparameter tuning appears limited to a coarse grid search (e.g., {0.1, 0.5, 1.0}) for each baseline SRL method, raising some concern that baselines (VAE, SPR) might be under-tuned relative to the proposed method, which could inflate the apparent gap.

The paper's claimed generality ("highly versatile and can be applied to a wide range of tasks") is only tested on WBC-style locomotion/imitation; no manipulation or more complex embodied tasks are evaluated despite motivating the work with manipulation and dynamic-environment interaction.

Presentation clarity could be improved: some figures (e.g., Figure 9, 10) have small/dense subplots that are hard to parse, and the interval-update mechanism explanation in the main text is somewhat terse relative to its apparent empirical importance.

strengths: Addresses a relevant and underexplored problem: systematically studying state representation learning (SRL) for humanoid whole-body control, which has received less attention than SRL in other RL domains.

Provides an open-source modular framework (SRL4Humanoid) that decouples SRL and RL updates and implements multiple SRL paradigms (reconstruction/VAE, dynamics/SPR, contrastive/SimSiam) with a consistent interface, which could be useful to the community for reproducible comparison.

Reasonably extensive empirical study, including ablations on update interval, training data proportion, which encoder (policy vs. value) receives the SRL loss, computational overhead, and the weighting coefficient lambda.

Goes beyond simulation-only evaluation with a Sim2Sim validation on MuJoCo and qualitative Sim2Real deployment on a physical LimX Oli humanoid, and appendix experiments on an additional robot (Unitree G1) and a rough-terrain variant task.
Comparison against a teacher-student distillation baseline (TSD) in the appendix, which is a natural alternative method for leveraging privileged information.
weaknesses: The fairness of the core comparison is unclear: the paper's main claim is that PvP's advantage comes from jointly leveraging proprioceptive and privileged states, yet the appendix descriptions of the VAE and SPR baselines (Eqs. 10-11) show them operating on observations/state-action pairs without an explicit mechanism for incorporating privileged state information as PvP does. If the baselines are not given equivalent access to privileged information, the comparison does not isolate the effect of the proposed contrastive objective versus simply having privileged information available, undermining the central claim.

The technical novelty is incremental: PvP is essentially a SimSiam-style contrastive objective applied between proprioceptive and privileged state embeddings, closely related to the cited PIM method (contrastive SRL from a single modality) and to standard asymmetric actor-critic (privileged critic) designs already common in legged robot RL. The paper does not clearly articulate what is technically novel beyond extending contrastive learning to two modalities with zero-masking.

Evaluation breadth is limited for the main results: only two tasks (velocity tracking, motion imitation) on one robot platform are used for the primary analysis; the additional rough-terrain and Unitree G1 experiments are relegated to the appendix with less detailed analysis, and all core findings essentially come from a single humanoid platform (LimX Oli).

Statistical rigor is weak: the number of random seeds used to produce mean/std shaded regions is not reported, and no significance testing is provided. In several plots (e.g., Figure 5 right, Figure 9 velocity task) the baseline curves largely overlap, so the claimed consistent advantage of PvP is not strongly substantiated visually.

Real-world evaluation is purely qualitative (keyframe images in Figure 1 and text description); no quantitative tracking error, success rate, or robustness metrics are reported for the physical robot, limiting the evidentiary strength of the 'real-world deployment reliability' claim central to the paper's motivation.

The normalized score metric used throughout the main results is not precisely defined (e.g., normalization reference bounds), making it difficult to judge the practical magnitude of reported improvements.

The introduction motivates the work with broader humanoid capabilities (manipulation, balance, multi-task locomotion), but the evaluation is restricted to velocity tracking and motion imitation, which is narrower than the scope implied by the motivation.

strengths: Introduces a simple and well-motivated contrastive learning formulation (PvP) that pairs proprioceptive and privileged states via zero-masking augmentation, avoiding hand-crafted data augmentation typically needed by contrastive SRL methods.

Provides SRL4Humanoid, a modular open-source framework implementing multiple representative SRL paradigms (reconstruction-based VAE, dynamics-based SPR, contrastive SimSiam) alongside PvP under a unified PPO backbone, which is useful for the community and supports fair comparison.

Extensive empirical study across two main tasks (velocity tracking, motion imitation) plus appendix experiments on rough terrain and a different robot platform (Unitree G1), with ablations on training time proportion, training data proportion, SRL application to policy vs. value encoder, and computational overhead.
Comparison against teacher-student distillation baselines (TSD) in the appendix strengthens the positioning of PvP relative to a well-established alternative for leveraging privileged information.
Includes both Sim2Sim (MuJoCo) validation and real-world deployment on the LimX Oli humanoid, which is a meaningful reproducibility/robustness signal beyond pure simulation results.
The paper is clearly written, the architecture and loss formulation (Eq. 2-6) are explained precisely, and hyperparameters/network architectures are reported in the appendix for reproducibility.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is a relatively incremental adaptation of SimSiam (a well-established contrastive learning method) to a new pair of modalities (proprioceptive vs. privileged state) rather than a fundamentally new representation learning mechanism; novelty is primarily in the application/instantiation.

Real-world evaluation is entirely qualitative (images/videos); no quantitative real-robot metrics (e.g., tracking error, success rate, energy usage) are reported to substantiate claims of improved real-world deployment reliability.

The number of random seeds used to produce the mean/std curves is not stated anywhere in the main text or appendix, making it hard to assess the statistical robustness of the reported improvements, especially given the large variance in Figures 5-9.

Task diversity is limited to velocity tracking and motion imitation on largely flat terrain (with one rough-terrain variant in the appendix); broader manipulation or highly dynamic contact-rich tasks are not evaluated, which limits generalizability claims.

Comparisons are restricted to internally-implemented SRL baselines (VAE, SPR, SimSiam) and TSD; no comparison to recent state-of-the-art humanoid WBC frameworks (e.g., HugWBC, BeyondMimic mentioned in related work) is performed on the same benchmark, so it is unclear how PvP's absolute performance compares to current best practice.

The choice and sensitivity of privileged-state composition (e.g., which subset of privileged information is used for pairing) is only partially explored; the impact of selecting different privileged features on PvP performance is not systematically studied.

The interval-update mechanism (Eq. 6) and its hyperparameter T are introduced somewhat ad hoc to fix an observed instability, but the paper does not deeply analyze why an update interval of 50 is generally optimal, limiting the generality of this practical guideline.
